ap_statistics-m01.stem: In an observational study of $240$ employees, researchers found that those who work from home tended to have higher productivity ratings. Which of the following is a possible confounding variable?

options.text: The productivity rating of each employee
options.why: The response variable itself is not a confounding variable.

options.text: The number of employees who responded
options.why: Sample size does not vary with the explanatory or response variable.

options.text: The color of the office walls
options.why: Unrelated to both variables, so it cannot create a false association.

options.text: The type of job the employee has
options.why: Jobs that can be done at home may differ in how productivity is rated, which affects both variables.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Identify a confounding variable in an observational study
student_thinking: Recall that a confounding variable is related to both the explanatory variable and the response variable
Reject options that are the response itself, are unrelated to both variables or are only a feature of the study

key_conditions.condition: a confounder is associated with both the explanatory and the response variables
key_conditions.evidence: the stem describes an observational study with an explanatory and a response variable

misconceptions.description: names a variable unrelated to both

verification.independent_path: each scenario is written with exactly one variable linked to both variables and three named non-confounders drawn from a fixed catalog that was checked by hand for uniqueness

ap_statistics-m02.stem: A random sample of $150$ customers of a grocery chain found that $74$ of them buy store-brand products. A $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all customers of a grocery chain who buy store-brand products is $(0.413,\ 0.573)$, and the conditions for inference are met. Which is the correct interpretation of this interval?

options.text: $95\%$ of all samples of customers of a grocery chain will have a sample proportion between $0.413$ and $0.573$
options.why: Confuses the confidence interval for the population proportion with the sampling distribution of the sample proportion.

options.text: There is a $95\%$ probability that the proportion of all customers of a grocery chain who buy store-brand products is between $0.413$ and $0.573$
options.why: Treats the fixed population proportion as random: the probability statement describes the method, not this particular interval.

options.text: We are $95\%$ confident that the proportion of all customers of a grocery chain who buy store-brand products is between $0.413$ and $0.573$
options.why: A confidence interval estimates the population proportion; the confidence level describes the method, and the interval is stated about the population proportion in context.

options.text: We are $95\%$ confident that the proportion of the customers of a grocery chain in the sample who buy store-brand products is between $0.413$ and $0.573$
options.why: Describes the sample proportion, which is already known exactly, instead of the population proportion that the interval estimates.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Interpret a confidence interval for a population proportion in context
student_thinking: Identify the parameter the interval estimates: the proportion of the whole population, not of the sample or of future samples
Choose the statement that describes the confidence level as confidence in the method and names the population in context

key_conditions.condition: a confidence interval is interpreted as confidence that the interval captures the population parameter
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the sample counts and the interval and says the conditions are met

misconceptions.description: assigns a probability to the fixed parameter
describes the sample instead of the population

verification.independent_path: the interval is recomputed with the z critical value from statistics.NormalDist (independent of scipy.stats.norm) and the large counts condition is verified

ap_statistics-m03.stem: A city official claims that $0.4$ of residents support building a new park. In a random sample of $200$ residents, the sample proportion who support the park is $0.459$. A test of $H_0: p = 0.4$ versus $H_a: p > 0.4$ gives a P-value of $0.044$. The curve shown models the sampling distribution of the sample proportion when $H_0$ is true, and the shaded area is the P-value. Which is a correct interpretation of the P-value?

stimulus.description: Sampling distribution of the sample proportion when H0 is true with the upper tail shaded

options.text: The probability that the true proportion is $0.4$, given the sample proportion of $0.459$, is $0.044$
options.why: Interprets the P-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true, but it is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true.

options.text: If the true proportion were $0.4$, the probability of getting a sample proportion of exactly $0.459$ by chance alone is $0.044$
options.why: Uses exactly the observed value instead of the observed value or something more extreme in the direction of the alternative.

options.text: If the true proportion were $0.4$, the probability of getting a sample proportion of $0.459$ or larger by chance alone is $0.044$
options.why: The P-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true and gives the chance of a result at least as extreme as the observed sample result.

options.text: The probability that the true proportion is greater than $0.4$, given the sample proportion of $0.459$, is $0.044$
options.why: Interprets the P-value as the probability that the alternative hypothesis is true, which a significance test does not give.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Interpret a P-value in the context of a test for a proportion
student_thinking: Recall that the P-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true
Choose the statement that gives the probability of a result at least as extreme as the observed one under that assumption, not the probability of a hypothesis

key_conditions.condition: the P-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis is true, of a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed
key_conditions.evidence: the stem gives the hypotheses, the sample proportion and the P-value, and the figure shades the upper tail

misconceptions.description: reads the P-value as the probability that H0 is true
reads it as the probability that Ha is true
uses exactly the observed value instead of at least as extreme

verification.independent_path: the upper-tail area is computed from math.erf and the shaded region and marked value are generated from the same sample proportion and standard error as the P-value

ap_statistics-m04.stem: A least-squares regression of hot drinks sold (cups) on outdoor temperature (degrees Celsius) for $13$ observations gives the computer output shown. Which is the best interpretation of the slope of the regression line?

stimulus.description: Computer output for a least-squares regression

options.text: For each additional cup, the predicted temperature decreases by about $3.240$ degree Celsiuss
options.why: Reverses the roles of the explanatory and response variables.

options.text: For each additional degree Celsius, the number of hot drinks sold decreases by exactly $3.240$ cups
options.why: Treats a prediction from a fitted line as an exact change instead of a predicted change on average.

options.text: For each additional degree Celsius, the predicted number of hot drinks sold decreases by about $3.240$ cups
options.why: The slope $b=-3.240$ is the predicted change in the response for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable.

options.text: When the temperature is $0$, the predicted number of hot drinks sold is about $-3.240$ cups
options.why: Confuses the slope with the intercept: the predicted value at zero is the intercept.

blueprint.subject: ap_statistics
blueprint.concept: Interpret the slope of a least-squares line in context from computer output
student_thinking: Read the slope from the coefficient in the row of the explanatory variable, not from the constant row
Interpret it as the predicted change in the response for each one-unit increase in the explanatory variable

key_conditions.condition: the slope is the predicted change in y for each one-unit increase in x
key_conditions.evidence: the output lists the constant and the slope coefficient with the variable names and units

misconceptions.description: confuses the slope with the intercept

verification.independent_path: the least-squares slope is recomputed from the closed-form sums of deviations and compared with numpy polyfit; the coefficient shown in the output is the rounded fitted value
